title: Transmission of Heat

notes.heading: 1. Steady-State Conduction, Fourier's Law & Thermal Resistance Analogy
notes.proseLatex: In 1D steady state (every cross-section at time-independent temperature), heat current $H = \frac{dQ}{dt} = \frac{KA(T_1 - T_2)}{L}$ ($\text{W}$) mirrors Ohm's law $I = \frac{\Delta V}{R}$ with thermal resistance $R_{\text{th}} = \frac{L}{KA}$ ($\text{K/W}$) and thermal conductivity $K$ ($\text{W\,m}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}$). Series slabs share identical heat current $H$ ($R_{\text{eq}} = R_1 + R_2$), whereas parallel rods share identical $\Delta T$ ($1/R_{\text{eq}} = 1/R_1 + 1/R_2$).

keyFormulas.label: Fourier Heat Current, Thermal Resistance & Series Conductivity
keyFormulas.latex: $H = \frac{KA\Delta T}{L} = \frac{\Delta T}{R_{\text{th}}},\quad R_{\text{th}} = \frac{L}{KA},\quad K_{\text{series, }L_1=L_2} = \frac{2 K_1 K_2}{K_1 + K_2}$
keyFormulas.aiExplainContext: Solve junction temperature and equivalent conductivity of series/parallel composite slabs.

examples.problemLatex: Two slabs of equal area and equal thickness with conductivities $K_1 = 300$ and $K_2 = 100\text{ W\,m}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}$ have outer faces at $100^\circ\text{C}$ and $0^\circ\text{C}$. Find steady interface temperature $T_j$ and $K_{\text{eq}}$.
stepsLatex: Equal $H$: $K_1(100 - T_j) = K_2(T_j - 0) \implies 3(100 - T_j) = T_j \implies T_j = 75^\circ\text{C}$.

notes.heading: 2. Convection & Newton's Law of Cooling
notes.proseLatex: Convection transports heat via bulk fluid motion (natural buoyancy-driven vs forced fan/pump-driven; natural convection vanishes in zero-gravity orbit!). For small excess temperature above ambient $T_0$, Newton's law of cooling states $-\frac{dT}{dt} = b(T - T_0)$, whose interval-average form $\frac{T_1 - T_2}{\Delta t} = b\left(\frac{T_1 + T_2}{2} - T_0\right)$ solves JELET cooling-time questions in two lines.

keyFormulas.label: Newton's Law of Cooling (Average Form)
keyFormulas.aiExplainContext: Compare successive cooling intervals rapidly using midpoint excess temperature.

examples.problemLatex: A body cools from $80^\circ\text{C}$ to $70^\circ\text{C}$ in $5\text{ min}$ in a $30^\circ\text{C}$ room. How long does it take to cool from $70^\circ\text{C}$ to $60^\circ\text{C}$?
stepsLatex: Interval 2: $\frac{10}{\Delta t} = b(65 - 30) = 35b \implies \Delta t = 5\times\frac{45}{35} = \frac{45}{7}\text{ min} \approx 6.43\text{ min}$.

notes.heading: 3. Thermal Radiation: Kirchhoff, Stefan-Boltzmann & Wien's Displacement Law
notes.proseLatex: Radiation needs no material medium and propagates at $c = 3\times 10^8\text{ m/s}$. Kirchhoff's law equates spectral emissivity and absorptivity ($e_\lambda = a_\lambda$; good absorbers are good emitters, with ideal blackbody $e = a = 1$). Stefan-Boltzmann gives radiated power $P = e\sigma A T^4$ (net exchange with enclosure at $T_0$ is $e\sigma A(T^4 - T_0^4)$ with $T$ in KELVIN!), and Wien's law $\lambda_m T = b \approx 2.898\times 10^{-3}\text{ m\,K}$ shifts peak wavelength toward blue as $T$ rises.

keyFormulas.label: Stefan-Boltzmann T⁴ Law & Wien's Displacement Law
keyFormulas.latex: $P_{\text{net}} = e\sigma A(T^4 - T_0^4),\qquad \lambda_{\max} T = b = 2.898\times 10^{-3}\text{ m\,K}$
keyFormulas.aiExplainContext: Convert Celsius to Kelvin before raising to T^4 and apply Wien peak-wavelength scaling.

wbjeebTraps: ABSOLUTE KELVIN TRAP: in Stefan's $T^4$ and Wien's $\lambda_m T = b$, NEVER plug $^{\circ}\text{C}$ directly — always convert $T(\text{K}) = t(^\circ\text{C}) + 273$!
Equal-thickness series slabs give harmonic mean $K_{\text{eq}} = \frac{2K_1 K_2}{K_1+K_2}$, whereas equal-area PARALLEL slabs give arithmetic mean $\frac{K_1+K_2}{2}$.
Cooling from $70^\circ\text{C}\to 60^\circ\text{C}$ ALWAYS takes LONGER than cooling from $80^\circ\text{C}\to 70^\circ\text{C}$ because excess temperature $(T - T_0)$ shrinks.

conceptPrimer.heading: Fourier's Law & the Electrical Analogy
conceptPrimer.proseLatex: Steady-state 1D conduction: heat current $H = \frac{KA(T_1 - T_2)}{L}$ (watts) mirrors Ohm's law with thermal resistance $R_{\text{th}} = \frac{L}{KA}$ ($\text{K/W}$). Series slabs carry the SAME $H$ with $R_{\text{eq}} = \sum R_i$; parallel rods share the SAME $\Delta T$ with $\frac{1}{R_{\text{eq}}} = \sum\frac{1}{R_i}$. Micro-check: $K = 0.2$, $A = 1$, $L = 0.1$, $\Delta T = 50$: $H = 100\,\text{W}$.

conceptPrimer.heading: Series vs Parallel Effective Conductivity
conceptPrimer.proseLatex: Equal-thickness series slabs: $K_{\text{eq}} = \frac{2K_1K_2}{K_1+K_2}$ (HARMONIC mean — dominated by the poor conductor). Equal-area parallel: $K_{\text{eq}} = \frac{K_1+K_2}{2}$ (arithmetic mean). Micro-check: $K_1 = 0.2$, $K_2 = 0.6$ in series: $K_{\text{eq}} = \frac{0.24}{0.8} = 0.3$; in parallel: $0.4$.

conceptPrimer.heading: Convection & Newton's Law of Cooling
conceptPrimer.proseLatex: Convection moves heat by bulk fluid motion (natural vs forced; zero-$g$ kills natural convection). Small excess temperature: $-\frac{dT}{dt} = b(T - T_0)$; the interval form $\frac{T_1 - T_2}{\Delta t} = b\left(\frac{T_1+T_2}{2} - T_0\right)$ solves cooling-time questions in two lines. Micro-check: cooling is SLOWER at lower excess temperature: $70\to60$ takes longer than $80\to70$.

conceptPrimer.heading: Kirchhoff's Radiation Law
conceptPrimer.proseLatex: $e_\lambda = a_\lambda$ at thermal equilibrium: good absorbers are good emitters; a blackbody has $e = a = 1$. A white/reflective surface both absorbs AND emits less. Micro-check: a rough blackened bulb cools faster by radiation than a polished one in the same room.

conceptPrimer.heading: Stefan–Boltzmann & Wien's Displacement
conceptPrimer.proseLatex: $P = e\sigma AT^4$ with $T$ in KELVIN (the classic trap); net exchange with surroundings at $T_0$: $P = e\sigma A(T^4 - T_0^4)$. Wien: $\lambda_m T = 2.898\times10^{-3}\,\text{m K}$ — hotter bodies peak bluer. Micro-check: doubling $T$ (K) multiplies $P$ by $16$; $T = 290$: $\lambda_m \approx 10\,\mu\text{m}$ (infrared).

conceptPrimer.heading: Radiation Needs No Medium
conceptPrimer.proseLatex: Radiation propagates at $c = 3\times10^8\,\text{m/s}$ through vacuum — the only transfer mode that works across empty space (Sun to Earth). Conduction needs matter contact; convection needs bulk flow. Micro-check: a vacuum flask kills conduction/convection; radiation remains, cut by silvering.

Using arithmetic mean for series slabs.
Claiming temperature is constant along a series rod.

Ignoring the $-T_0^4$ term for net exchange.
Using the single-slab resistance without adding series layers.
